title: Texas chili
subtitle: Beef chili con carne without beans
excerpt: Texas-style chili: beef braised low and slow in a deep chile sauce of dried ancho and guajillo peppers, cumin, and beef stock. No beans. No tomatoes. Nothing but beef and red chiles in a thick, rich sauce.
sourceNotes: Texas-style chili con carne (also called chili Colorado or bowl of red) has no beans and no tomatoes. The tradition descends from the chili stands of San Antonio and is codified in the International Chili Society competition rules. Cross-referenced with Robb Walsh, The Chili Cookbook (2015).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes for up to 3 months. The flavour improves after freezing.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well with no change to technique.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made a day ahead. The spices bloom further overnight.

content.text: Texas chili is a different dish from chili con carne with tinned tomatoes and kidney beans. This version builds its sauce from reconstituted dried chiles, which give a flavour that is earthy, fruity, and deeply spiced without the acidity of tomatoes. Dried ancho and guajillo chiles are available in specialist Mexican grocery shops and online. The beef is cut into chunks, not minced.
Toast the dried chiles in a dry pan over medium heat for 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Do not let them burn. Place in a bowl and cover with 400 ml hot stock. Soak for 20 minutes until softened.
Transfer the softened chiles and their soaking liquid to a blender. Blend until smooth. Strain through a sieve to remove any remaining skin or seeds. Set aside.
Season the beef generously. Heat the oil in a large heavy casserole over high heat. Brown the beef in batches without crowding the pan, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Cook the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and spices and cook for 1 minute.

Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the chile sauce and the remaining 200 ml stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to very low. Cover and cook for 2 to 2.5 hours, stirring every 30 minutes, until the beef is very tender and the sauce has thickened and darkened.
If using masa harina to thicken, dissolve it in a little cold water and stir in during the last 20 minutes. Cook uncovered to finish.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve in deep bowls with soured cream and grated cheddar.

items.cause: Dried chiles were over-toasted or burned
items.fix: Toast chiles just until fragrant; 30 seconds is enough. Burned chiles are very bitter and cannot be rescued.

items.symptom: The sauce is not thick enough
items.cause: Too much liquid or cooked with the lid on
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final 30 minutes to reduce. Add a masa harina slurry to thicken quickly.

items.cause: Not cooked long enough or heat too high
items.fix: Continue on the lowest possible heat. Chuck needs a full 2.5 hours to become tender.

items.cause: Ancho and guajillo are mild chiles
items.fix: Add a pinch of cayenne or one dried chipotle to the sauce before blending.

content.text: Texas chili is the subject of fierce regional pride. Beans are explicitly excluded from the classic version, as are tomatoes; both are considered adulterants by serious Texas chili cooks. The dish descends from the chili stands operated by Mexican women in San Antonio in the 1880s, and has evolved into its own form: a sustained braise in a chile-based sauce with no shortcuts. It is judged at competitions with strict rules. Served over rice, in a bowl with crackers, or as the base for a Frito pie.
